note: These are looks that came out of particular economic and political conditions: postwar rubble, Weimar inflation, revolution, class resentment, Cold War censorship. That gives them a built-in argument about who gets seen and how. They differ mainly in how much they trust the real world (neorealism, kitchen-sink, Dogme) versus how much they distrust it (Expressionism, montage, Czech satire). Nothing was checked on the web for this entry, so engine notes are working knowledge of Flow, Nano Banana and Veo to be tested, not verified facts.
left_out: Japanese golden age and Japanese New Wave (Ozu, Kurosawa, Oshima): strong but covered partly by other families
Indian parallel cinema and Bollywood masala: very different, worth its own entry
Third Cinema and Latin American militant cinema (Hour of the Furnaces, Memories of Underdevelopment): highly relevant politically, left out for space
New Hollywood 1970s (Taxi Driver, Network, The Conversation): usable, but close to common AI 'gritty film' defaults
Free Cinema documentary shorts and Humphrey Jennings' wartime British documentaries: folded partly into British social realism
Nollywood and Iranian post-revolution cinema (Kiarostami): distinct but less verified for prompting
Berlin School and contemporary European slow cinema

note: These are looks that cinema built to serve one kind of story: noir for corruption, the western for lone justice, the paranoid thriller for institutions. Each carries a built-in worldview, so picking one imports its politics and its moral shape as well as its lighting. Check that the genre's assumptions fit the argument before you commit. All eight are rendered through Flow, where the frame is 16:9 or 9:16, so ratios like 1.37:1 and 2.39:1 are done in post. No searches were run; everything here is from working knowledge, so the engine notes are stated cautiously and should be tested.
left_out: Courtroom and procedural drama: flat, institutional framing with a lot of talking; usable but close to the 1970s paranoid thriller visually and hard to make visually varied
Cold War spy drama (grey, tobacco-stained, wide interiors, a la Smiley-era British TV): overlaps with the paranoid thriller and the dystopia entries
Italian giallo: saturated coloured gels and stylised murder set-pieces, strong look but violence-centred and likely to hit policy blocks
1980s/90s neon action and cyberpunk: very over-represented in AI output already, so not a useful addition to the menu
Hammer/gothic horror: candle-lit saturated colour; a cousin of folk horror but less tied to land and class
Epic/sword-and-sandal and Biblical Technicolor spectacle: useful for empire and ruler satire, but a large-cast cost problem
Screwball and Ealing-style comedy: closer to the British social comedy family than to genre cinematography, but excellent for working-class satire

note: These are looks where the viewer can see a human hand (thumbprints, scissor edges, brushstrokes, eraser smudges) and where the medium's limits become part of the voice. For a UK working-class audience that tangible, small-scale, made-in-a-shed quality can read as honest and warm, which is useful cover for dark satire. The shared engine problem is that Flow's models lean towards smooth, glossy, 3D-render-like output, so every style here needs to be pushed away from clean CGI and towards stepped motion, real materials and visible imperfection.
left_out: Sand animation on a lightbox (Caroline Leaf's The Owl Who Married a Goose, 1974): close to paint-on-glass, so folded in rather than separate
Czech and Eastern European object and found-material surrealism (Jan Svankmajer's Dimensions of Dialogue, 1982): very distinctive but sits between puppet and clay and is hard to prompt
Hand-drawn watercolour animation (e.g. Isao Takahata's The Tale of the Princess Kaguya, 2013): omitted as it is closer to drawn animation than hand-made craft, and too costly to hold consistent
Direct-on-film / scratch animation (Len Lye, Norman McLaren): abstract, rarely suited to narrative satire
Needle-felted wool and fibre animation: beautiful but a close cousin of textured puppet stop-motion
Cardboard and recycled-junk stop-motion (e.g. Michel Gondry's cardboard sets): a lo-fi variant of the puppet and clay styles

note: These are all styles where the image is openly designed rather than photographed: flat shapes, drawn lines, pixels, polygons, paper cut-outs or diagrams. That makes them forgiving for generators, because they don't depend on photoreal detail. It also makes them risky, because the generic AI default (glossy, smooth, soft-lit) is the thing most likely to leak back in. Each entry says which kind of argument it carries and which it would undermine. Note: no web searches were run; every reference and engine claim comes from established knowledge, and the engine notes are behaviours to test in a first round, not guarantees.
left_out: Rotoscope animation (Waking Life, A Scanner Darkly): painted-over live action; strong for dreamy unease, but needs live footage as input.
1-bit and dithered monochrome (Return of the Obra Dinn): very distinctive but narrow, and close to pixel art.
Corporate flat vector ('Memphis' explainer look): deliberately left out as the default AI-generic trap, not a style to choose.
Whiteboard/hand-drawn explainer: folded into the infographic entry (RSA Animate).
Isometric diorama / tilt-shift miniature: usable for system overviews but thin on emotional range.
Eastern European poster-graphic animation (Zagreb school): close to UPA but with a harder political edge; a candidate for a later pass.
Chibi / cute anime sub-styles: not suited to this audience and tone.

note: These are looks borrowed from things that were printed or drawn by hand: flat ink, limited colour, hard outlines, and typography that does the arguing. Their shared strength is that they say "this is a point of view" before a word is spoken, and they hide the generator's usual weakness (photographic mush) by working in simplified shapes. Their shared risk is motion: Veo wants to add depth, shading and camera parallax, which kills the flatness that makes the style work.
left_out: Manga / shonen-seinen comic style: very usable but a tonal outlier for this UK audience and well covered elsewhere
WPA-adjacent mid-century modern flat vector (Saul Bass-style title design): more a design movement than print
Soviet socialist realist painting poster: overlaps constructivism but heavier and more nostalgic
Punk photocopy collage / cut-and-paste zine (Jamie Reid-style ransom note collage): strongly British and politically fitting, worth its own entry
Peter Kennard-style political photomontage: close to constructivist photomontage
1930s American editorial newspaper cartoon with crayon texture
Tarot / medieval illuminated manuscript marginalia: a less obvious candidate
Pop-art halftone comic (Ben-Day dots)
Japanese ukiyo-e woodblock print

note: These styles borrow the composition rules, light logic and colour discipline of a painting tradition and apply them to a moving frame. What joins them is that each carries a built-in attitude to power and ordinary people (sympathy, menace, irony, heroism, mockery), so choosing one is choosing an argument as well as a look. They split broadly into painterly-lit styles (Dutch, Hopper) that survive Veo's photoreal bias, and flat or graphic styles (ukiyo-e, Pop, Lowry, muralism) that fight image-to-video and need careful motion design. Notes in this library were written from the researcher's own knowledge; no web searches were used, so engine-behaviour claims are general and should be tested with a cheap still round before committing.
left_out: Surrealism (Magritte-style plain-object dream imagery): strong for satirical visual metaphors, left out to avoid overlapping with Pop and Expressionism
Bauhaus and Constructivist design (grids, primary shapes, photomontage): close to Pop and Socialist Realism graphically but very different in feeling
Art Nouveau (whiplash line, floral frames, poster lettering): decorative, good for a sarcastic 'belle epoque' narrator but low on political content
Georgian and Victorian caricature (Hogarth, Gillray, Cruikshank): British political satire in print; possibly the closest tradition to BadCode's tone, and worth its own entry
Kitchen Sink realism painting and social-realist photography of the 1950s-60s: grounded UK domestic grit
Impressionism and Post-Impressionism: broken colour and light; rarely fits political satire
Futurism and Vorticism: speed, machines and angular dynamism; good for energy but a narrow fit
Dada photomontage (Hoch, Heartfield): collage as political weapon, strong fit but overlaps Pop collage and is hard to animate

note: These eight are photographic ways of looking, each with its own claim about what a picture is evidence of: a place, a crowd, a crime, a lifestyle, an institution. That claim is what makes them usable for satire, because the story can borrow the credibility of the genre and then break it. They are mostly still-image idioms, so animating them in Veo costs something. Movement tends to wash out the very thing that defines them (the frozen instant, the grain, the flash), so most of them work best as held plates with small, motivated motion.
left_out: Decisive-moment humanist street photography (Cartier-Bresson, Maier, Winogrand): folded into the documentary entry; would be a distinct entry with more room
Daguerreotype and early-photography portraiture: covered by the wet-plate entry
1990s-2000s British fashion and youth-culture editorial (i-D, The Face, Corinne Day): excellent for youth and class but needs separate research
Press photojournalism of strikes and protest (miners' strike, Poll Tax): partly covered by documentary, could stand alone
Disposable-camera and early digital point-and-shoot snapshot aesthetic (2000s Britain): a strong candidate for a modern-day entry
Kodachrome slide-projector family archive: overlaps with the instant-film entry
Aerial and satellite imagery: more a data-image tradition than photography proper

note: These styles borrow the look of a recording technology and the authority (or intimacy, or menace) that audiences already attach to it: newsreels sound official, home movies sound private, CCTV sounds like being watched. For a satirical project that claims to be received wisdom from a future that went wrong, that borrowed authority is the main asset. The shared risk is that generators render these as a filter on a clean image rather than as the real constraints of the medium (aspect ratio, lens, lighting, tape or film behaviour), and every entry says where it fails and what it would undermine.
left_out: Early webcam / dial-up internet (Geocities, MSN-era low-frame-rate webcam video, 56k pixel art): distinct and usable, cut for space; strong for a story about the 1998-2008 internet
Silent-era hand-coloured Pathecolor or Kinemacolor: overlaps with the tinted silent film entry
Open University / 1970s educational broadcast with diagrams and corduroy lecturer: close to the 1970s TV and public information entries
Home-computer era graphics (ZX Spectrum, BBC Micro loading screens): a screen-graphic texture similar to teletext
Cold War-era Super 16 documentary / 1960s cinema verite handheld: a neighbour of newsreel
Dashcam / bodycam / phone-vertical footage: modern surveillance family, covers a different era
Polaroid and magazine-print photo textures (stills only): overlaps with archive stills but not a moving-image medium

note: These styles borrow the grammar of a format the audience already knows from the sofa or the phone, so the viewer arrives with a set of rules and the story can break them for effect. The strength is instant recognition and a built-in tone (deadpan, gravity, cosiness, hype, intimacy). The shared risk is that each format carries its own authority and its own politics: a mockumentary laughs at its subjects, a natural-history voice sounds neutral when it isn't. Pick the grammar whose attitude matches who you want the viewer to blame.
left_out: Reality TV / docusoap with confessional booth and manufactured-drama edit (close to mockumentary but with producer-led cuts and ominous stings)
Rolling news and breaking-news broadcast (lower-third tickers, studio anchor, live-link reporter), strong for satire but overlaps game-show graphics and screen-life
Found-footage and CCTV/bodycam (surveillance grammar, timestamps, low-res grain)
Sitcom multi-camera studio comedy with laugh track
Cooking, property and makeover shows (Location Location Location style), relevant to housing satire
Talking-heads explainer / Vox-style video essay with motion graphics
Teletext and Ceefax screen grammar

note: These styles all announce that the picture was made by hands on a stage or a table: puppets, paper, cloth, cardboard, cut photographs. That visible artifice is the family's gift to satire, because it lets the image say "this is a model of the argument" and lets caricature, scale and cruelty read as craft rather than realism. The shared risk with generators is that they smooth the handmade away, so every entry needs explicit material language and a deliberate protection of the seams.
left_out: Paper diorama and toy theatre (Victorian Pollock's-style layered card stage) - overlaps silhouette, cut-out and cardboard entries
Punch and Judy / seaside booth glove puppetry - very British and class-relevant, but narrower than the entries chosen
Stop-motion clay and plasticine (Aardman-style) - belongs in an animation family
Tableau vivant and painted-history staging (Greenaway-style) - overlaps with epic-theatre-black-box
Marionette and string puppetry as its own entry - partly covered via Team America and Thunderbirds references
Lego/brick animation - partly covered by the DIY and miniature entries

family: British and Irish folk and roots
note: These are the musics of work, pub, chapel, picket line and street, made by and for people with little money, so they already carry class as part of their sound. What joins them is a voice that tells a story in plain words over simple, repeated forms, which suits satire about economics. They split into communal (shanty, brass band, music hall singalong), lonely (unaccompanied ballad), driving (skiffle, folk-rock) and argued (protest, Radio Ballad) registers, and the choice mostly decides whether the audience is invited to join in, to listen, or to be told off.
left_out: Irish pub session and rebel ballad group (Dubliners/Planxty style): overlaps electric folk, shanty and protest folk and is the most obvious Irish pick
Scots mouth music (puirt a beul) and Gaelic waulking song: striking and less obvious, but narrow for a UK-wide working-class audience
Northern Soul-adjacent working men's club cabaret and brass-and-organ club sound: more pop than folk
Morris and country dance music (melodeon, tabor): strongly rural and comic, risks twee
Gospel-tinged Welsh male voice choir and chapel hymnody: very strong for class and mining but needs careful handling to avoid cliche
Contemporary acoustic punk-folk (Pogues-style) and Britpop-era folk pop: a hybrid more than a distinct tradition

note: These styles share a lineage: Caribbean sound-system culture (dub, ragga) met British council estates, pirate radio and cheap sequencers, and each decade rebuilt it at a new tempo (jungle 160-170, garage 130-135, grime and dubstep 138-142, drill 140-145). Almost all of it is made for a room with a big low end and a crowd, which makes the sub-bass a character in its own right, and most of it is about place and class from the inside. They split on one axis that matters for BadCode: whether a voice is in front (grime, drill, garage, bassline) or whether the music is a bed under a voice (dub, trip-hop, dark dubstep, jungle instrumentals).
left_out: Liquid and neurofunk drum and bass: the clean 174 BPM descendant of jungle, with melodic, polished or industrial sub-styles; close to jungle in tool prompts so not given its own entry
Speed garage and 4x4 UK garage: a faster, house-leaning cousin of 2-step, partly folded into the garage and bassline entries
Road rap and UK hip-hop (boom-bap British rap): a lyrical, sample-based tradition distinct from grime and drill, belonging more with a hip-hop family
Afroswing and UK funky: warm, Afro-diasporic, dance-leaning UK sounds that are less about bass pressure and political satire
Breakbeat hardcore and happy rave: euphoric 1991 to 1993 pre-jungle rave, usable for nostalgia but weaker for political argument
Post-dubstep and UK bass/'future garage': a moody electronic offshoot of dark garage and dubstep, currently well represented by the early-dubstep and garage entries

note: These are British guitar-band traditions from 1971 to 1995, each a different answer to how a band that is not the elite can sound like it speaks for itself. They run from shouted solidarity (Oi!, 1977 punk, pub rock) through cold analysis (post-punk) and comic observation (Britpop) to retreat (shoegaze, jangle) and spectacle (glam). Most were made on cheap kit by working-class or art-school kids, which suits BadCode's reader, but each carries a stance that can help or undermine a satirical argument.
left_out: Garage rock (1960s Nuggets-style and 2000s revival): raw and fuzzy, but largely American-coded and fewer class specifics
Riot grrrl: feminist punk with strong politics but US-centred and a different audience framing
Madchester/baggy: indie-dance fusion of the late 80s, distinct but more about the dancefloor than guitars
Krautrock/motorik: German, adjacent to post-punk's groove but not in this lineage
Art-rock (Roxy Music, Talking Heads, Radiohead): wide and mood-driven, overlaps with post-punk and glam
Folk-punk and 'Rock Against Racism' reggae-punk crossover (The Specials, 2 Tone ska): directly working-class and political, but ska may belong to another family

note: These styles all put the words first: the voice is the lead instrument and the beat is a bed that lets a sentence be heard. They differ mainly in where the voice sits (rapped on the grid, ranted off it, or spoken against it), which place the accent says you are from, and how much the music argues with the words. For a UK working-class audience the accent and register are the point, since they say whose side the story is on. Caveat: written without live web searches, so references come from memory (titles and years are ones I am confident exist) and the Suno notes are general engine behaviour, not tested for this project; verify with a small test round before locking a style.
left_out: Horrorcore and abstract/underground rap (El-P style dense production), unusual but heavy in tone
Drill (UK/Chicago), a menacing cousin of trap that is tied to real violence and best avoided for satire
Jazz rap and lo-fi hip-hop as a bed for narration
Rap-musical / theatrical rap (Hamilton-style) with sung book numbers
Talking blues and folk talking-song traditions (Woody Guthrie style) that sit between spoken word and folk
Rap-rock / rap-metal fusion (Rage-style political fury)
Cloud rap and emo rap, introspective rather than political

note: All of these are built from machines rather than bands, so they share a cold, exact surface that can carry either deadpan authority or sudden warmth. They differ most in where the voice sits (up front, buried, or absent) and in whose past they evoke (Thatcher-era pop, German motorway, rave field, a half-remembered school film). For a narrator who speaks with total authority from the future, this family is natural: the machine is the narrator's own native sound.
left_out: Techno (Detroit / Berlin): overlaps with acid house and EBM, and it is largely wordless and structure-light
IDM / glitch (Autechre, Squarepusher): too dense and unpredictable for narration beds, and hard to steer in Suno
Italo disco / Hi-NRG: a possible bright, camp alternative to synth-pop
Dub techno / Basic Channel style: a hypnotic, spacious cousin of ambient and motorik
UK garage / 2-step and grime-adjacent electronic: strongly relevant to a UK working-class audience, but sits closer to the dance/urban family
Vaporwave / plunderphonics: a sample-decay style close to hauntology
Berlin-school sequencer music (Tangerine Dream): a long-form arpeggio cousin of motorik and synthwave

note: These styles share acoustic instruments, written-out arrangements and a sense of occasion: the music arrives sounding like it has authority, tradition or a ritual behind it. That makes the family strong for irony (solemn form carrying a savage or silly message) and weak when a story needs to sound casual, current or street-level. No web searches were run for this entry; engine notes below come from known Suno behaviour and should be confirmed by listening tests, and the story's sound.md should record what actually happened.
left_out: Gregorian chant and plainchant: a single unaccompanied line, strong for ritual and a future-cult register, but narrower than the entries chosen.
Neoclassical/ambient piano and strings (post-classical): popular as underscore but overlapping with minimalism and string quartet.
Early music and Renaissance consort (viol, lute, madrigal): distinct and usable for satire of the court, but near baroque.
Choral-orchestral spectacle (Carmina Burana, O Fortuna type): a hybrid of choir and late-romantic orchestra, heavily used by trailers.
Tragic verismo opera: sung grief and betrayal, partly covered by the requiem and comic-opera entries.
Modernist and avant-garde (Ligeti, Xenakis, Penderecki clusters): strong for dread, but inaccessible to the target audience.
Fanfare and military band: a close cousin of the brass band, more official in tone.
Film orchestral hybrid: cinematic orchestra plus electronics, which belongs in a film-score family rather than this one.

note: These are styles built to serve a scene, a character or an audience in a room, so they carry plot, attitude and theatrical irony more readily than a pop song does. They split into two camps. Voice-led forms (cabaret, patter, music hall, book-musical, workers' chorus) put the words first and suit argument. Score-led forms (western, spy, suspense) put atmosphere first and suit narration beds and underscore. None of this is verified by live search; engine notes are working knowledge of how Suno responds to descriptive prompts and should be tested with the variations skill.
left_out: Pantomime proper (dame, villain boo, audience call-and-response) folded into the music hall entry rather than given its own
Disney and animated-musical ballad style: usually too warm and sentimental for this brief
Silent-film cinema organ and silent-comedy piano accompaniment
Ealing comedy and British post-war light orchestral score (brass band and strings with jaunty clarinet)
Kitchen-sink and 1970s British TV drama library music and Radiophonic Workshop electronic cues
Gothic Hammer horror orchestral score
Blaxploitation and 1970s funk film soundtrack
Opera buffa and Rossini-style comic opera patter (close relative of Gilbert and Sullivan)

note: These styles share one engine: a song is a way for people with no power to say a hard thing out loud together, using call-and-response, a blue-note vocabulary and rhythm that carries the message when the words are not safe. That makes the family the most natural fit BadCode has for songs about work, debt and who owns what, and also the one where a careless imitation reads as costume. The family ranges from solo and unaccompanied (field recordings, delta blues) to huge ensembles (big band, mass choir), so it covers almost every scale of story. No reference below was searched during this run; all are works I am confident exist, and the Suno behaviour notes are described tendencies, not tested results.
left_out: Bebop and hard bop small-combo jazz: fast, complex, and mostly instrumental, so less useful for story songs.
Deep Southern soul (Stax and Muscle Shoals): raw, horn-led and emotional; close to Motown but grittier.
Chicago electric blues: amplified, band-driven, urban; a sibling of delta blues.
Doo-wop and street-corner vocal groups: close harmony and nonsense syllables, good for comic choruses.
Ragtime and early New Orleans jazz: lively and ironic but dated for most stories.
Spirituals and sorrow songs in concert-arrangement form (as sung by university choirs).
Early hip-hop and boom-bap: Black American but a separate family of its own.

family: Global traditions with UK roots or reach
note: These are the sounds that arrived in Britain on boats, planes and sound systems and were remade here, mostly by working-class kids in Coventry, Handsworth, Brixton, Southall and Birmingham. Most of them were already political or communal music before they reached a studio, so they carry a stance as well as a groove, and a story that borrows one inherits that stance. I did not run any web searches. Every reference below is from memory and I am confident each exists, but some release years are approximate and flagged as such.
left_out: Klezmer: Jewish diaspora wedding music with a small British scene; distinctive clarinet-led sound, but weaker UK-working-class connection than the entries chosen.
Fado: Portuguese melancholy song with some UK diaspora reach; very distinct, but the 'saudade' register is narrow and has no UK-rooted political tradition.
Highlife: West African dance-band music that fed British Afrobeat and the 1950s London scene; overlaps heavily with the afrobeat entry.
Cumbia: Colombian cumbia has a London scene (and Latin-American migrant communities) but its UK roots are thinner than the entries here.
Irish rebel ballad and ceili: strong UK working-class reach, probably belongs in a British folk family instead.
Jungle, drum and bass and UK garage: British-born Caribbean-diaspora sounds, probably belong in an electronic family.
Gospel and Black British church choir music: strong UK roots and a collective voice, but better covered in a vocal/choral family.
Qawwali and Bollywood film song in the UK: widespread British Asian reach, but long-form devotional qawwali is a poor fit for satire.
Soca: the fast carnival descendant of calypso, left out because it overlaps with the calypso entry in how Suno handles it.

family: Novelty, found sound and the margins
note: These are the forms where the sound itself carries a social meaning before a single lyric lands: the shop jingle, the playground rhyme, the terrace roar, the safety film, the library cue. Most of them are things a UK working-class listener has heard thousands of times without ever choosing to, which makes them strong vehicles for political satire (familiar form, hostile content) and weak vehicles for sincerity unless that gap is the point. What joins them is that they are functional or collective music: made to sell, to teach, to scare, to be shouted, or to sit under something else. That is also where Suno is weakest, because it is trained toward finished, polished, single-voice songs.
left_out: Ska and 2-tone novelty (Specials-type political pop) - belongs more with protest pop than novelty
Spoken-word with drone (poetry-over-bed) - closer to narration scoring than a margin style
Radiophonic Workshop synth cues as a distinct style from musique concrete (Derbyshire, Oram, Hodgson)
Hymn and church-parody (hymn tunes with new words) - covered partly by the terrace chant
Sea shanty and work song - folk family
Hold music, elevator and lift music (muzak) - strong satirical candidate for corporate dread
Radio ident and station-jingle pastiche
Bedroom lo-fi tape-hiss/cassette-recording aesthetic as a found-sound medium
